lf: Kauaʻi's main lava flows date from 5.6 to 3.8 million years ago, making it the oldest of the main Hawaiian Islands.
Kauaʻi rises from the Hawaiian hotspot
Oʻahu's main lava flows erupted 3.4 to 2.2 million years ago as the Pacific Plate carried it off the Hawaiian hotspot.
Oʻahu's volcanoes build a new Hawaiian island
Molokaʻi's main lava flows date from 1.8 to 1.3 million years ago.
Maui's main lava flows are 1.3 to 0.8 million years old, built by the Haleakalā and West Maui volcanoes.
Maui's volcanoes rise from the Pacific
Hawaiʻi Island's surface lavas are less than 700,000 years old, and the island is still growing over the hotspot.
The Big Island of Hawaiʻi begins to rise
Mauna Loa first erupted on the seafloor 0.6 to 1 million years ago and probably broke the ocean surface about 300,000 years ago.
Mauna Loa breaks the ocean surface
Kīlauea's first lavas erupted onto the seafloor 210,000 to 280,000 years ago.
Kīlauea begins erupting on the seafloor
This undersea volcano began growing about 400,000 years ago; its summit is still about 975 m below the waves. It may be Hawaiʻi's next island.
The sharp bend in the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain formed roughly 50 to 42 million years ago, when the hotspot track changed direction.
Española first rose above the sea about 3.2 million years ago, making it one of the oldest Galápagos islands.
Española, among the oldest Galápagos islands, rises
Fernandina, about 700,000 years old, is one of the youngest and most active Galápagos islands.
Fuerteventura's oldest rocks above sea level are about 20.2 million years old, the oldest in the Canary Islands.
Fuerteventura, the first Canary Island, rises
Teide and its twin Pico Viejo have grown inside Tenerife's Las Cañadas caldera over about the last 170,000 years.
El Hierro's lavas above sea level are less than 1.1 million years old, making it the youngest Canary Island.
Santa Maria rose from the sea about 6 million years ago, sank partly under it, then rose again.
Santa Maria, the oldest Azores island, rises
Réunion's Piton des Neiges volcano rose above the sea about 2 million years ago after growing on the seafloor.
Réunion rises from the Indian Ocean
Piton de la Fournaise became active more than 500,000 years ago and is now one of Earth's most active volcanoes.
Mauritius's oldest volcanic rocks are thought to be about 10 million years old; its youngest basalts are only about 20,000 years old.
Tristan da Cunha is roughly 200,000 years old; its volcanic peak rises 2,060 m and last erupted in 1961.
Ascension began erupting on the seafloor about 6 million years ago but only rose above the sea in the last million years.
Jeju began forming in eruptions about 2 million years ago and is topped by Hallasan, South Korea's highest peak.
Anak Krakatau, the "child of Krakatau", first broke the surface in 1927 inside the caldera left by the 1883 blast.
Anak Krakatau rises from the sea where Krakatoa blew apart
A new island 120 m high formed between two Tongan islets in early 2015; the January 2022 eruption destroyed it.
A new volcanic island forms in Tonga
A new island broke the sea surface near Nishinoshima in November 2013 and had swallowed the old island by March 2014.
Parícutin was born in a Mexican cornfield on 20 February 1943 and grew to 424 m before it stopped erupting in 1952.
Parícutin volcano is born in a Mexican cornfield
Surtsey burst from the Atlantic off Iceland in November 1963 and grew for three and a half years; scientists have watched life settle it since.
Surtsey rises from the sea off Iceland
Etna began erupting about 500,000 years ago and has grown to about 3,300 m, Europe's tallest active volcano.
Somma-Vesuvius began erupting less than 39,000 years ago; its present cone grew inside the Somma caldera after 79 CE.
Fuji's present cone, Younger Fuji, began growing about 11,000 years ago on top of Older Fuji.
Younger Fuji begins to build today's cone
Kilimanjaro's oldest centre, Shira, began erupting about 2.5 million years ago; its summit cone Kibo was built 274,000 to 170,000 years ago.
Today's Mount Rainier was built from hundreds of lava flows over the last 500,000 years.
Mount St. Helens began erupting about 40,000 years ago; its 1980 blast lowered the summit by about 400 m.
Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago, forming the caldera of Crater Lake, 592 m deep.
Mount Mazama collapses; Crater Lake fills its caldera
Yellowstone's latest caldera formed 640,000 years ago in the Lava Creek eruption, about 1,000 km³ of ash and rock.
Toba's supereruption about 74,000 years ago left the 100 km caldera that holds Lake Toba.
Ngorongoro's caldera formed 2 to 3 million years ago when a great volcano collapsed.
The main Deccan eruptions began about 250,000 years before the dinosaur extinction and poured out over 1 million km³ of lava.
The Deccan Traps pour lava across India
From 16.7 million years ago, over 350 lava flows buried 210,000 km² of the Pacific Northwest.
Columbia River flood basalts bury the Pacific Northwest
Lava from fissures that opened in August 2014 spread over 84 km² by early 2015.
Holuhraun lava field spreads across Iceland
Kīlauea's 2018 eruption buried 35.5 km² in lava and added about 875 acres of new land to Hawaiʻi.
Kīlauea's lower Puna eruption adds new land to Hawaiʻi
A 24 km crater blasted 14.8 million years ago; Nördlingen's St. George's Church is built from its shocked suevite rock.
An asteroid blasts the Ries crater in Germany
An asteroid hit about 36 million years ago, carving a 100 km crater and turning graphite into impact diamonds.
An asteroid carves the 100 km Popigai crater in Siberia
About 35 million years ago a meteorite hit here, leaving an 85 km structure now buried under the bay.
A meteorite strikes where Chesapeake Bay will be
An iron asteroid about 46 m across struck about 50,000 years ago, blasting a crater over 1,200 m wide and 210 m deep.
An iron asteroid blasts Meteor Crater in Arizona
An asteroid struck just over a million years ago; its crater now holds Ghana's only natural lake, sacred to the Asante.
An impact forms the Bosumtwi crater in Ghana
About 570,000 years old, Lonar is a rare impact crater in basalt, its 1.8 km bowl now filled by a lake.
The Laramide orogeny began raising today's Rocky Mountains roughly 70 million years ago.
India rammed into Asia 40–50 million years ago, and the Himalayas are still rising more than 1 cm every year.
25 million years ago central Tibet held a low valley; later uplift built the flat Roof of the World.
Africa and Europe collided 40–50 million years ago; the Matterhorn's upper walls are a slab of African-plate crust.
The Alps begin to rise as Africa meets Europe
As Iberia pushed into Europe, the central Pyrenees rose and eroded fastest about 35–30 million years ago.
The Pyrenees rise between Iberia and France
Between 10 and 6 million years ago the Andean plateau rose from under 2 km to about 4 km high.
The Altiplano surges upward in the Andes
Arabia's collision with Eurasia raised the Greater Caucasus, with most of the uplift in the past 5 million years.
Starting about 25 million years ago, the East African Rift began splitting Africa; it now runs about 3,500 km.
The East African Rift begins to split Africa
About 31–29 million years ago, floods of basalt covered 600,000 km² here, up to 2 km thick in places.
Flood basalts build the Ethiopian Highlands
The Red Sea rift's main phase came about 20 million years ago; new ocean floor began forming about 5 million years ago.
The Red Sea rift tears Arabia from Africa
Afar began rifting about 25 million years ago where three rifts meet; its Erta Ale volcano holds an active lava lake.
Baja began tearing away from Mexico about 10 million years ago; the sea flooded the gap by about 8 million years ago.
The sea floods into the new Gulf of California
Active for about 20 million years, this fault has slid Arabia about 105 km past Africa.
Iceland's oldest surface rocks, in the Westfjords, are about 16 million years old; the island straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Iceland's oldest rocks erupt on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Antarctica iced over about 34 million years ago, after carbon dioxide in the air fell roughly 40 percent.
Opening around 34 million years ago, the Drake Passage let the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, Earth's strongest current, circle Antarctica.
The Drake Passage opens between South America and Antarctica
Soil frozen beneath Greenland's summit for 2.7 million years shows the ice sheet's centre likely never fully melted since.
Dune deposits about 7 million years old in Chad are the oldest known evidence of the Sahara desert.
The first Sahara dunes form in Chad
Cosmogenic dating suggests the Atacama's core turned hyperarid over 40 million years ago, among the driest places on Earth.
Dune 45 is built of sand about 5 million years old, and the Namib Sand Sea's tallest dunes tower over 300 m.
About 25 million years old and up to 1,642 m deep, Baikal is Earth's oldest, deepest lake, with about 20% of unfrozen fresh water.
Lake Baikal opens in a Siberian rift
Its central basins began forming 9–12 million years ago in the East African Rift; it is the world's second-deepest lake.
Lake Tanganyika begins to fill a rift basin
Formed about 1.36 million years ago, Ohrid is Europe's oldest continuously existing lake.
Lake Ohrid forms in the Balkans
About 12 million years ago the Paratethys became a megalake of 2.8 million km², home to dwarf whales about 3 m long.
The Paratethys becomes Earth's largest lake ever
About 2.8 million years ago the Isthmus of Panama fully joined North and South America.
The Bering Strait first opened about 5.5 million years ago, letting Pacific shellfish cross the Arctic toward the Atlantic.
The Bering Strait opens for the first time
The Colorado River linked older canyons into the Grand Canyon 5–6 million years ago; one segment is far older.
A 9.3-million-year-old lava flow shows the Sierra Nevada crest has tilted and risen about 2 km since it erupted.
Basalt-dated sediments show a river much like today's Yangtze was already flowing at least 23 million years ago.
The Yangtze River takes its course
About 9.4–9 million years ago the Amazon became a continent-crossing river, carrying Andean sediment to the Atlantic.
Mantle flow under Ethiopia may have kept the Nile flowing north for about 30 million years.
Fed by Himalayan erosion, the Bengal Fan is the world's largest submarine fan; drilled deposits reach back 23–24 million years.
By about 6500 BCE rising seas drowned Doggerland, cutting Britain off from mainland Europe.
Rising seas drown Doggerland; Britain becomes an island
As Doggerland drowned, the Dogger Bank hills survived as an island in the North Sea until about 5000 BCE.
About 8,200 years ago a huge undersea slide off Norway sent a tsunami across the North Sea and over low Doggerland.
The Storegga slide sends a tsunami across the North Sea
Lake Bonneville covered over 50,000 km² of the Great Basin; Utah's Great Salt Lake is its shrunken remnant.
About 18,000 years ago Lake Bonneville burst out at Red Rock Pass, peaking near 1 million m³ of water per second.
The Bonneville Flood bursts out of Red Rock Pass
Bigger than today's Great Lakes combined; its final drainage about 8,200 years ago may have raised the sea 1–3 m.
Lake Agassiz drains into the ocean
Rising seas drowned the land bridge to the mainland, making Tasmania an island about 12,000 years ago.
Rising seas make Tasmania an island
Seas rose about 120 m after the last ice age, drowning half of Sundaland and splitting it into today's islands.
Mediterranean water spilled through the Bosporus into the Black Sea; one study dates it to about 7,600 years ago, but how fast it happened is debated.
The Mediterranean spills through the Bosporus into the Black Sea
Rising seas reflooded the Gulf basin and reached about today's level some 7,000 years ago.
Rising seas refill the Persian Gulf
From about 11,000 to 5,000 years ago the Sahara held grassland and lakes; rock art shows giraffes and hippos.
The Sahara turns green with grass and lakes
About 7,000 years ago Lake Mega-Chad covered over 400,000 km², slightly larger than today's Caspian Sea.
Lake Victoria dried out about 17,000 years ago and refilled around 14,700 years ago as rains returned.
Lake Victoria refills after drying out
Its final outburst near Billingen, Sweden, about 11,600 years ago dropped the lake about 25 m to sea level.
After the Baltic Ice Lake drained, salt water entered and formed the Yoldia Sea about 11,700 years ago.
About 10,700 years ago the Baltic became a freshwater lake again as the land rose faster than the sea.
From about 7,500 to 4,000 years ago a saltier Littorina Sea filled the Baltic basin.
Nevada's Lake Lahontan reached its last highstand about 14,500 to 13,000 years ago; Pyramid Lake is a remnant.
About 8,000 years ago the sea flooded ice-crushed land around Hudson Bay, up to 250 km inland of today's shore.
Today's living reef is under 10,000 years old, the latest of at least five reefs here in 30,000 years.
Today's Great Barrier Reef begins to grow
As sea-level rise slowed around 6500–5500 BCE, Nile silt began building the fertile delta plain.
The Nile begins building its delta
For the last 1,200 years or so the Mississippi has built its birdfoot-shaped delta into the Gulf.
Since its 1750 maximum, Glacier Bay's ice has retreated about 65 miles, opening a new fjord to the sea.
Glacier Bay's ice begins its great retreat
After a major flood in 1787 the Brahmaputra took a new course, the Jamuna, abandoning its old channel.
The Brahmaputra jumps to a new course, the Jamuna
The New Madrid quakes of 1811–12 dammed the Reelfoot River and flooded a forest; old stumps still stand underwater.
New Madrid earthquakes create Reelfoot Lake
In 1855 the Yellow River broke its bank at Tongwaxiang and swung north to the Bohai Sea.
Changes in the course of the Yellow River
The Yellow River swings north to a new mouth
In 1905 the Colorado River broke through an irrigation canal, creating what is now California's largest lake.
The Colorado River floods in to form the Salton Sea
A 1911 quake-triggered rockslide built a natural dam about 600 m high, backing up a lake about 60 km long.
A rockslide dams the Bartang River, forming Lake Sarez
Six years after the 1913 Los Angeles Aqueduct opened, Owens Lake was nearly completely dry.
Owens Lake dries up after the Los Angeles Aqueduct
The Afsluitdijk, finished in 1932, sealed off the salty Zuiderzee and turned it into a freshwater lake.
Lake Mead began filling behind Hoover Dam in 1935 and became America's largest reservoir.
East Flevoland (1957) and South Flevoland (1968) were drained from the sea, adding about 958 km² of land.
East Flevoland is drained from the sea
Once the world's 4th-largest lake, the Aral Sea shrank after 1960s river diversions; its eastern basin dried out in 2014.
The Aral Sea begins to shrink as rivers are diverted
Lake Chad shrank about 90%, from about 26,000 km² in 1963 to under 1,500 km² decades later.
The Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, backed the Nile into Lake Nasser, about 550 km long.
The Aswan High Dam fills Lake Nasser
Begun in 2001 from sand dredged off the seafloor, Dubai's palm-shaped island took shape by late 2003.
Dubai begins building the Palm Jumeirah island
In August 2008 the Kosi burst its banks into a channel abandoned over 200 years earlier, flooding Bihar.
The Kosi River jumps its banks into an old channel
